title: Wrestling till daybreak (Genesis 32:22–32)
hookLine: Jacob wrestles all night, won't let go without a blessing, and limps away renamed
carry: I will not let thee go

lines: TWENTY YEARS, AND ESAU IS COMING.
ALONE BY A RIVER, IN THE DARK.
cards: In a side chapel of the church of Saint-Sulpice in Paris, there's a huge painting by Eugène Delacroix. A tree twists up into the sky.
In front of it, two figures are locked together: a man, muscles straining, pushing with everything he has, and one with wings, standing almost calmly, a hand on the man's thigh.
Twenty years have passed since Jacob ran from home. He's rich now, with wives, children, flocks. Tomorrow he has to face the brother who once planned to kill him, coming with four hundred men.
Tonight, alone by a river, someone grabs him in the dark.

teach.h: A MAN, AN ANGEL, OR GOD?
teach.b: First, the fight. Jacob sends his family across the river Jaboc and stays behind alone, and a man wrestles with him until the breaking of the day. Who is he?
Genesis just says a man. The prophet Hosea later calls him an angel. Jacob, by morning, says he has seen God face to face.
The text leaves it open, and so does Delacroix. Second, the hold. The stranger can't overcome him, so he touches the hollow of Jacob's thigh, and it's put out of joint.
Then, in the Douay-Rheims: "Let me go, for it is break of day. He answered: I will not let thee go except thou bless me."
Injured, exhausted, and still holding on. Third, the name. The stranger asks, what is thy name?
For the man who once said I am Esau to his father, the answer is a confession: Jacob.
Heel-grabber. And the stranger says: "Thy name shall not be called Jacob, but Israel: for if thou hast been strong against God, how much more shalt thou prevail against men?"
Israel, in Hebrew, sounds like one who strives with God, or God strives. A whole people will carry the name of a man who wrestled with God and wouldn't let go. Fourth, how the Church reads it.

teach.h: PRAYER AS A BATTLE OF FAITH.
teach.b: The Catechism calls this scene a symbol of prayer as a battle of faith and a triumph of perseverance.

teach.h: I WILL NOT LET THEE GO.
teach.b: Jacob doesn't win by pinning anyone. He wins by holding on, and asking. And he walks away at sunrise blessed, renamed, and limping.

how: The Catechism points to Jacob's night at the river as a symbol of prayer as a battle of faith and a triumph of perseverance.

o: a prince of peace who rules the land
heel-grabber, the name Jacob was born with
one who strives with God, Jacob's new name

games.q: what's inside the long night — tap the pairs.

s: Genesis clearly says Jacob wrestled an angel
Genesis says a man. Hosea later says an angel. Jacob says he saw God face to face.
Jacob refuses to let go without a blessing
"I will not let thee go except thou bless me."
Jacob wins by pinning his opponent
the stranger puts his hip out of joint. Jacob wins by holding on, and asking.

games.q: you've wrestled a stranger all night. your hip is out of joint. dawn is coming and he says: let me go. what do you do?
o: hold on: I will not let thee go except thou bless me.
ask him to heal your hip first.
games.why: Jacob holds on and asks for a blessing. he's given a new name, Israel, and walks away at sunrise, limping.

practice: Bring up something you've been wrestling with, a decision, a grief, a question about God, and instead of letting go after a moment and reaching for something easier, stay with it through the whole bell.
You don't need to win; just keep hold. If you pray, you can use Jacob's words: I will not let thee go.

wordCard.voice: Israel. The new name Jacob is given after wrestling all night: one who strives with God. It becomes the name of a whole people.

orig.note: Hebrew: Israel, usually explained as one who strives with God, or God strives.
